summary: Paula McLain's Modern Love essay, published March 12, 2021 in The New York Times, explains why she took a vow of celibacy unrelated to religion after a messy two-year relationship. She ties her difficulty with sex and love to childhood sexual abuse in foster care, her sisters' separation from their chaotic family, and her years of self-destructive dating after aging out of the system. She describes her second year of self-imposed celibacy as an effort to stop fighting the same war and to accept her wounds without self-blame.
one_line: Paula McLain explains her non-religious vow of celibacy as a break from patterns of love and sex rooted in childhood trauma and foster care.
key_facts: Paula McLain took a vow of celibacy twenty months before the essay was published, and the vow had nothing to do with religion.
The essay was published March 12, 2021, in the Modern Love column of The New York Times.
McLain was 5 when she and her two sisters were sent to live with a couple in the foster care system in Fresno, Calif.
McLain's sisters were 3 and 7 years old at the time they entered that foster home.
McLain's mother had skipped town with a boyfriend the year before without saying goodbye.
McLain said she was molested by the husband in the foster home, and she was 7 when the family was taken away after she spoke up.
McLain told her therapist, "I just want to have some other argument with the universe," when she decided to swear off relationships.
McLain wrote that after aging out of the system at 18, she broke ties with her foster family and her biological family and made a policy of never telling anyone how she had grown up.
McLain enrolled in community college and rented an apartment with her sisters, living paycheck to paycheck well below the poverty line.
McLain wrote that she often felt herself sliding out of her body during sex, "like watching a mannequin going through the motions."
McLain wrote, "Sex scared me, so I had more of it."
McLain's essay concludes that she did not break herself and that she wants to carry her experiences rather than wish for a different story.
McLain is the author of the novel "The Paris Wife," and her new novel "When the Stars Go Dark" was to be published in April 2021.
